WE’RE HIRING: Quantitative Rates Researcher | Remote Global

Position: Quantitative Rates Researcher
Openings: 100
Job Type: Contractor
Location: Remote Global
Compensation: $80–$150/hr

ABOUT THE ROLE

micro1 is engaging Quantitative Rates Researchers to support a leading investment bank’s algorithmic trading platform project.

You’ll apply your expertise in fixed income and rates markets to help train next-generation AI systems. No prior AI experience is required — your domain expertise is what matters.

WHAT YOU’LL DO

* Review and assess AI-generated quantitative research and trading strategy outputs.
* Identify methodological issues such as lookahead bias, overfitting, data snooping, and unrealistic transaction cost assumptions.
* Evaluate backtesting frameworks, including rates-specific carry/roll-down mechanics and contract roll conventions.
* Scrutinize signal construction, factor modeling, and alpha research.
* Assess statistical rigor and research methodology.
* Provide detailed written feedback on model assumptions, implementation fidelity, and research quality.
* Collaborate asynchronously with project coordinators to clarify findings and recommendations.
* Help improve research evaluation processes for greater accuracy and relevance.

REQUIRED QUALIFICATIONS

* Quantitative research, analysis, or consulting experience in fixed income or rates markets.
* Experience building or backtesting systematic rates strategies at a hedge fund, asset manager, or bank.
* Advanced proficiency in Python with pandas, NumPy, and SciPy, or R.
* Strong understanding of yield curve modeling, carry/roll-down analytics, and relative value trading.
* Knowledge of SOFR/Eurodollar instruments and Treasury futures.
* Strong statistical and quantitative research skills.
* Ability to evaluate transaction costs, liquidity constraints, and real-world trading conditions.
* Exceptional attention to detail and written communication skills.

PREFERRED QUALIFICATIONS

* Experience assessing quantitative models against industry best practices.
* Strong understanding of factor modeling, alpha research, model validation, and systematic strategy backtesting.
* Experience identifying methodological issues including lookahead bias, overfitting, and data snooping.

HIRING PROCESS: 100% VIRTUAL

With 70+ million people using Linktree and 48,000 new accounts created every day, the surfaces you build reach an enormous and varied audience - and the integrations you ship are often the reason someones Linktree becomes the one link that does everything. Most of all, youll help Linktree achieve our mission: to empower anyone to curate and grow their digital universe.   What Youll Own  Design, build and ship full-stack features across the Linkapps surface, from the partner-facing services through to what the creator actually sees.  Own third-party integrations end-to-end: evaluate the partners API or SDK, design the integration, ship it, and keep it healthy in production.  Ship inside our composable Link Apps system, and improve it where you hit its edges, so that the next integration costs less than the last one did without turning every integration into a platform project.  Design and maintain the services, APIs and cloud infrastructure behind these experiences, with real attention to auth, rate limits, versioning and graceful degradation.  Partner with product, design and partnerships to work out whats technically feasible with a given partner and where the creator value actually sits.  Instrument what you ship and use the data to decide what to fix, cut or double down on.  Bring AI into how you build, and where it earns its place, into the integrations themselves.  Contribute to a strong engineering culture in a small, distributed squad - clear writing, good reviews, and leaving the codebase better than you found it.    Who Were Looking For  5+ years of professional software engineering experience shipping production full-stack features.  Solid full-stack skills across our core stack

This is why workforce strategy needs to be part of the transformation conversation early one.

For leaders, this means looking beyond headcount and planning for the capabilities needed to deliver today and frictionlessly in the future. The GCC’s digital ambitions demand more than investment in technology. They demand equal attention to the people who make it work.

WORKER PROTECTION AND HIRING

Portugal's 2009 reform aimed to encourage permanent employment by restricting fixed-term contracts at new establishments of large firms.

Researchers found that fixed-term hiring in those establishments fell. But they found no positive effect on permanent hiring. Large employers also opened fewer new establishments.

The story does not end there. Small firms in the same labour markets gained opportunities to hire. So the result for one group of employers was not the same as the result for the whole economy.

In the authors' 2023 study, the aggregate estimate changed when other firms' responses were included. A later model by the same authors changed both the size and the direction of the estimate.
The lesson is not that workers should go unprotected. It is that policymakers need to assess how specific rules affect both the security of existing jobs and the creation of new opportunities.

Prompt engineering isn't a side skill. It's part of the architecture.

Most people treat prompts as the last step: write something, test a few messages, ship.

On the AI features I've built, I treat the prompt as a design decision, the same as an API contract or a database schema 👇

1. Tone is a requirement.
A salon's WhatsApp bot and an admin lookup bot shouldn't sound the same. Each bot gets its own voice, because each one speaks for a different business.

2. Scope matters as much as capability.
A good bot knows what it should not answer. I define what's in scope up front, so it doesn't improvise outside it.

3. Guardrails go in early.
For customer-facing AI, the question isn't "can it answer?" but "what happens when it shouldn't?" That belongs in the first design, not a later patch.

4. In RAG, retrieval comes before wording.
Tuning the prompt won't fix bad retrieval. I tune what gets retrieved first, then the instructions around it.

5. Tokens are a cost.
Tighter prompts and better context retrieval mean fewer tokens and a more predictable system.

The shift for me was simple: a prompt isn't text you hope works. It's logic you design, test, and maintain.

Curious how others handle this. Do you treat prompts like code, with versioning and review, or more like config?

Cheap AI, Costly Mistakes: Why AI Governance Is Now a Business Topic

A few years back, using AI needed a data science team and a big budget. Today, any employee can sign up for an AI tool in two minutes, paste data into it, and get work done.

This is wonderful for productivity. It is also a serious risk that many leadership teams have not fully understood.
When AI becomes cheap and easy, it spreads quietly. Marketing uses one tool, HR uses another, developers use three more. Nobody has a full list. Nobody knows what data is going where.
And the mistakes are not small anymore. Customer data shared with an external tool. A chatbot giving wrong policy information to customers. A hiring tool with hidden bias. A contract summary that missed an important clause. Each of these can become a legal, financial or reputation problem.
That is why I feel AI governance can no longer sit only with the IT or legal team. It is a business topic, and it needs business leaders at the table.
Good governance does not mean blocking everything. Banning AI only pushes people to use it secretly. Instead, it means a few practical things:
A clear list of approved tools, so people know what is safe to use.
Simple rules on data. What can be shared, what can never be shared.
Human review for high-impact decisions, like hiring, lending, medical or legal matters.
An inventory of where AI is used across the company, updated regularly.
Training for employees, so they understand both the power and the limits.
One accountable leader who owns AI risk, with real authority.
The companies that get this right will move faster, not slower. When people know the guardrails, they experiment with confidence.
The cost of AI tools has come down sharply. The cost of AI mistakes has not.

Does your organisation have a clear AI usage policy yet?

For those of us wishing we had a crystal ball to predict what the future of employment might look like...

Quick disclaimer: Anthropic ran this study, wrote it up and published it about their own company. Take it with a grain of salt.

Second disclaimer: Anthropic is a coding and AI company, so some of this is going to land differently for them than it would for a non-tech business. Keep that in mind as you read.

Anthropic just published a report on how AI has changed work inside their own company over the past year or so. It’s long, so here’s the gist, good and bad:

- As of August, AI agents are working 6 hours for every 1 hour a human employee works there.
- Junior technical hiring has dropped off a cliff. The share of junior hires in technical roles fell from 27% to 9% in a year.
- Output is up across the board, not just engineering. Salespeople are closing more deals, lawyers are processing more contracts, accounts payable is clearing more invoices. Big disclaimer on this one though: Anthropic says themselves they can’t be sure how much of that is the AI versus their own product and business just booming at the same time.
- They checked for AI “slop” in the code, meaning low quality work that looks fine on the surface. No real difference found in the rate of bugs or rewrites compared to human written code.
- Meetings haven’t gone down, they’ve gone up. The average employee is spending 20% more time in meetings than a year ago. Even individual engineers, who you’d expect to be heads down coding more, are in 16% more meetings. Interesting...
- For non-technical staff, just reading everything their AI agents produce in a day would eat up over half their working week. So now there’s a whole new category of work just to manage and make sense of what the AI is doing.
- What hiring managers look for has shifted too. Less about specific technical skills, more about judgement, autonomy and whether someone can actually make a call.
- Anthropic is tracking which roles are most at risk internally and trying to move people into new roles rather than out the door. Though the report doesn’t pretend this fixes the real problem, which is that junior people aren’t getting hired in the first place.

I’ve seen most of the above happen in real time in AutoMATES too, but we’re a tech company with endless access to automations courtesy of Chris Metcalfe, so I know that’s not a fair comparison for most businesses reading this.

My eyebrows did raise when I read the phrase “managing teams of Claudes” in the report, but it tracks. I’ve got agents and automations running every day, and a chunk of my job now is just keeping an eye on them, fixing what breaks, deciding what they should and shouldn’t be doing. They take the boring work off my plate. What’s left for me is the strategy, the creative calls and the client relationships, the stuff that really needs a person.

A company that simulates air traffic and power grids for a living just raised $325 million at a $3 billion valuation.

ASI's pitch is simple: airlines, the US Army and the FAA already trust its models to tell them what's about to break before it does. The FAA signed an $875 million contract with them in June. That is not a chatbot deal, that is infrastructure people's lives depend on.

I keep coming back to this when I think about putting an AI agent inside a hiring loop. Air traffic control earned the right to use software through decades of simulation, redundancy and human override before anyone let it near a real decision. Most AI hiring tools got none of that runway. Demo to deciding who gets a callback, in about eighteen months.

We built Sunday narrow on purpose, screening and scheduling, not the final call, because I am not convinced hiring has earned the same trust air traffic control had to earn the hard way.

Where is the line for you? Is there a version of AI-run hiring you would actually trust with the final yes, or does that call stay human no matter how good the model gets?

Data salaries have doubled in 20 years.....

That’s the headline. I don’t think it’s 100% right..... 

So, I went back through 22 years of placement data from a desk that’s made around 3,000 placements, to see what actually moved. 

Same level, mid-2000s vs today (median base): 

- Analyst: $69k → $130k 
- Senior Analyst / Specialist: $94k → $138k 
- Manager: $105k → $165k 
- Head of / Director: $142k → $222k 

These are broad seniority bands. Most specific titles don’t have enough history to go back 22 years. 

Analysts have nearly doubled. Everyone else is up around 50%. That’s roughly 2% a year for most levels, closer to 3% for analysts. 

Wages generally have grown around 3%..... so most data roles have actually lagged.

But, it hasn't moved in a straight line: 

- 2004–2011: steady drift, even through the GFC 
- 2012–2019: the flat decade. Analyst pay sat at $90k for seven straight years 
- 2020–2023: the COVID jump. Biggest move in two decades 
- 2023–2026: the plateau. Like-for-like, flat for three years 

COVID did two things at once. Every business suddenly needed to understand its customers digitally, and closed borders cut off the overseas talent pipeline. 

Demand went up, supply down..... salaries had nowhere to go but up. 

Borders reopened, rates rose and hiring cooled. Pay didn’t fall back, but it hasn’t moved much since (outside a couple of areas, like AI). 

Here’s the curveball. 

Our average fee is up about 17% since 2023, with salaries flat.  

Clients are hiring more senior. Analysts were over half of our placements in the mid-2000s. Today it’s closer to a third. 

Anecdotally, there are fewer junior roles in the market full stop. That’s our read rather than hard data, but it’s consistent with what we’re seeing every day. 

Which raises the big question for me. If there are fewer graduate and junior jobs today, where does the next generation of managers come from? 

And will that shortage push base salaries up again in a few years’ time..... 

Who knows. But it’s one to watch. 

I have access to some really interesting data points beyond this. Contract rates, data governance, how specific roles have evolved over two decades. 

What would you like to see next? Let me know in the comments and I'll run the analysis, and overlay it with 16 years in market experience.

Let’s talk about the job market.

I’ll start with the ending: I found my next role using Claude, and by reaching out to a company that was NOT hiring.

I have more friends than I can count who are looking for a new role, and after 5+ rounds of interviews, weeks will go by before they hear anything. 

There are factors out of anyone’s control that make it a tough job market, but I think companies are hiring before they know what they’re looking for, and they’ve lost perspective on human connection.

-If someone reaches out to you on LinkedIn asking for help making a connection, reply. It takes 10 seconds, and one day it will be you asking, and I hope you get that support.
-If you’re putting someone through a culture fit conversation after 5 rounds of interviews across several time zones, and then deciding their technical skills don’t align, save everyone the time and figure that out after the first or second interview.
-If you tell a candidate you don’t know when you’re looking to hire, or ask if they’d be open to contract-to-hire, be concrete about what you mean. Or be honest, step back, and come back when you have real information. 
-If you’re interviewing someone, don’t make them wait a week plus for a 30-minute conversation. That waiting period is gruesome, and if you are truly ready to hire, it should not take very long to decide.
-Give honest feedback so people can do better next time. Not a fluff answer to save face. Set people up for success. 
-Reply to emails, someone on the other end is waiting for your response. (Still waiting on a few of you) 

And AI interviews? Who created these? That’s something I will never participate in. You want to potentially hire me, and you can’t even have a real conversation with me?
Companies need to do better, and the tools are already out there. Ashby, Workable, the list goes on. It’s 2026.
Instead of an AI interview, use AI to create an easier process for everyone involved, yourself included.

-So if you are one of those people who ignored someone’s message, go answer it and be a good human.
-If you are on a hiring team and you know deep down your company has a poor way of interviewing people, speak up.
-If you are looking for a job, don’t feel less than, because it has been literally every single one of us.
Help people, be the change, be the connector, be willing to speak up in a world where everyone tries to just fit in.

Stop pretending AI vendors are "neutral tech platforms." They are “algorithmic arms dealers” and the legal reckoning has arrived. Boom! 

For years, Silicon Valley sold a massive lie to corporate executives: "Buy our software, let it handle your hiring and firing, and if it blows up, blame the algorithm."

Well, the courts just blew up that defense. If you are a Founder, CEO, or CHRO, the era of using AI as a digital scapegoat to automate corporate cruelty is officially dead. 

Look at the receipts currently shattering the industry:

Mobley v. Workday: 
- Workday tried to argue in federal court that it couldn't be sued for employment discrimination because it’s just a tech platform. The judge's response? Absolutely not. The court ruled that because the AI actively screens, scores, and rejects candidates, the tech company legally acts as an "agent" of the employer. Tech vendors are now directly on the hook for Title VII civil rights violations.

- EEOC v. iTutorGroup
Think federal regulators are asleep at the wheel? The EEOC went full force after an automated system hardcoded to automatically reject older applicants, resulting in a $365,000 settlement and a harsh lesson: you cannot contract your way out of federal law using code.

- The FCRA Wave
AI companies that scrape employee data to generate secret "productivity scores" or "flight-risk metrics" are facing catastrophic class-actions. If an algorithm profiles a human to get them fired or skipped for a promotion without complete transparency, it's an illegal, unregulated background check. 

When an AI vendor packages systemic bias into a proprietary "black box" and sells it to your HR department, they aren't just a provider - they are a huge liability. And when the lawsuits hit, your organization and the tech bros who wrote the code will be sitting at the defense table together.

To the C-Suite and Founders: Here is how you protect your employees, your customers, and frankly, YOURSELF right now:

- Kill the Blind Trust: If you haven't forced your AI vendors to sign rigorous, legally binding indemnification clauses, you are holding a ticking financial time bomb. If their code breaks civil rights laws, their balance sheet needs to take the hit, not yours.

- Demand an Independent Bias Audit: Stop letting tech vendors grade their own homework. If they won't open up their "black box" to a third-party legal and technical audit, fire them immediately.

- Establish Human Veto Power: Never let an algorithm have the final say on hiring, firing, or promotion. If there isn't a qualified human actively reviewing and overturning automated decisions, you are practically begging for a class-action lawsuit.

You cannot outsource your ethics, and you cannot algorithm away your legal liability.
Get your compliance houses in order before a plaintiff's attorney does it for you.
And use humans! 
Happy Tuesday.

I know I’m not the only person who’s found themselves somewhere between the career they started with and the one they’re trying to build next. That kind of transition can be difficult to explain, especially for people coming from creative careers like mine, where so much of what you learn and build doesn’t fit neatly onto a résumé.

And while writing this has helped me make sense of my own path, I hope sharing my story also helps someone else navigating a similar change feel a little more seen.

For a long time, my life was music.

After graduating from Texas A&M with a finance degree, I boldly chose to become a recording artist, producer, engineer, and studio owner. I accumulated millions of streams and peaked at 400,000 monthly listeners - Spotify’s top 1% of artists.

There were plenty of wins. There were also songs that went nowhere, opportunities I thought would change everything that didn’t, and a lot of moments where I had to figure out whether I still believed in what I was doing.

Somewhere along the way, my relationship with music also got more complicated. When the thing you love becomes the thing you depend on financially, it can start to change the way you experience it. I found myself thinking more about whether a song would perform than whether I loved making it.

I’ll never stop making music. It’s too much a part of who I am. But as I’ve gotten older, my priorities have shifted. I’ve started valuing stability, consistency, and building a career that gives me more room to think long-term - both personally and financially.

I assumed prospective employers would value what I’d built. Instead, “artist,” “producer,” and “studio owner” didn’t translate on a résumé. That was humbling.

Ultimately, a roofing company gave me a chance. I knew nothing about the industry, but someone looked past my background.

Despite over 90% turnover on the sales team, I became its top performer. In my first 12 months, I generated $1.9M across 71 roofing contracts, sold remotely across 19 states.

When the company shut down 2 months ago, I was the last salesperson standing.

I left grateful, tested, proven, and excited for what’s next. 

Now I’m pursuing Account Executive, Business Development, Account Management, and client-facing growth roles, especially in tech, AI, music, and creative software.

If you know of a team looking for someone with sales ability, entrepreneurial experience, creativity, and a relentless work ethic, I’d be grateful for an introduction, referral, or even just a conversation.

And if we haven’t spoken in a while, I’d love to reconnect.

I know experience matters, but skills can be learned and systems taught. In the long run, how someone learns, adapts, shows up, and delivers results matters more.

I’m not asking anyone to overlook the experience I don’t have. I’m asking them to look more closely at the experience I do.

I guarantee you won’t regret hiring me.
